title: Keys and secrets: who can read them
standfirst: Three different things get called “secrets”: a value in an environment variable, a file on disk, and a placeholder that a proxy swaps for the real key on the way out. Only the third keeps the key away from the agent.

concept.heading: The agent can read what you give it
paragraphs: An agent runs as a process inside the machine, usually with root or sudo. Anything in its environment, any file on its disk, any credential in its home folder is something it can print, copy into a message, or send to a host an attacker controls. Agent 37 says this plainly in its own docs: anything in an instance's environment, the agent can read and repeat back.

That is fine when the agent is yours and the keys are low-value. It is not fine when you run an agent for someone else, or when the agent browses untrusted pages and can be talked into exfiltrating what it can see.

concept.heading: The placeholder pattern
paragraphs: The stronger design keeps the real value outside the machine. The sandbox gets a placeholder that looks like a key but is worthless on its own; an egress proxy recognises it on an outbound request and substitutes the real value, but only for the hosts you named. Runtime, boxd, InstaBox and Boat all offer some version of this.

The details decide how much it actually protects you. Which headers are rewritten? Runtime rewrites seven named headers and never URLs, so an API that takes `?key=` cannot use it. InstaBox's proxy handles HTTPS on port 443 only, with no body or URL substitution and no WebSocket upgrades. boxd's host-bound secrets are per host, and the machine holds a `bxds_` string. Boat's proxy is aimed specifically at model subscription logins, renewing Claude, ChatGPT and Grok sign-ins behind the proxy.

concept.heading: Where secrets leak without anyone attacking you
paragraphs: The common leak is a snapshot. InstaBox's home is `/data/home`, so a snapshot includes saved GitHub, Claude, Codex, git and SSH logins, and every machine built from that snapshot inherits them. Lizard's snapshot copies a volume's files and shares them with anyone who can restore it. boxd wipes in-VM agent logins the moment a machine is shared, which is a deliberate defence against exactly this.

The second leak is a shell that never loads the secret. InstaBox's secrets arrive through a profile script, so systemd units and `bash -c` without `-l` never see them. That is not a security hole; it is a support ticket.

comparisonIntro: Can the machine use a credential without being able to read it, and what are the limits of that protection?

rows.note: Instances boot with a per-instance token for four managed services (model router, search, Composio, Perflo), but there is no general secret manager: your own keys go in environment variables the agent can read.

source.quote: Anything in an instance's environment, the agent can read and repeat back.

rows.note: An “environment” injects variables, secret files and repositories into the VM, and removing a secret deletes it from disk. There is no broker and no short-lived credential exchange.

source.quote: Removing a secret from an environment and upgrading **deletes** it from the sandboxes' disks

rows.note: Two layers: sealed secrets injected at boot, and secrets bound to a host, where the machine holds an opaque `bxds_` string and the proxy swaps in the real key for that host only.

source.quote: Inside the machine `STRIPE_KEY` is an opaque string starting with `bxds_`.

rows.note: Org Secrets have a proxy mode: the sandbox sees `ibsec_…` and the real value is added only to HTTPS headers on port 443 to named hosts. Env mode exposes the value, and there is no body or URL substitution.

source.quote: Only in HTTPS request headers (port 443) to the Secret's `hosts`, where the outbound proxy swaps it in.

rows.note: Secrets are create-time environment variables that reach every command, plus a scoped CLI key per sandbox that dies with it. No proxy and no host binding.
The strongest version: the machine sees a placeholder, and the value is added only to HTTPS requests to the hosts you name. Plus OIDC tokens your AWS or GCP account can trust.

source.quote: The machine sees a placeholder. The value is added only to HTTPS requests to the hosts you name.

rows.note: Environment variables and secret files, a “safe for third parties” switch that withholds everything of yours, and an AI credentials proxy so sandboxes hold placeholder model keys.

source.quote: A placeholder is worthless outside boat. It does not contain the real key.

questions: Can the agent read the key, or only use it?
Which hosts can the key be sent to, and what happens with any other host?
Does the proxy rewrite headers only, or also URLs and request bodies?
Do secrets end up inside snapshots and forks?
Can I rotate a key without rebuilding the machine?
What happens if the agent is tricked into printing its environment?
Does a systemd service see the secret, or only an interactive login shell?

picks.situation: Run untrusted code or someone else's agent with my real API keys
picks.why: All three keep the real value out of the machine and scope it to named hosts. Runtime is the most explicit about what it rewrites and adds OIDC identity for cloud APIs.

picks.situation: Keep model subscription logins out of the box
picks.why: Boat renews Claude, ChatGPT and Grok sign-ins behind its proxy; Agent 37 injects a per-instance token for its managed model router. Both avoid putting a real subscription token on disk.

picks.situation: One trusted user, one box, simple setup
picks.why: Environment variables are adequate when the agent is yours and the keys are revocable. Neither offers a proxy, so budget time for rotation if a key leaks.

picks.situation: Different credentials per client or per end user
picks.why: All three scope secrets to an organisation, a label or a sandbox. boxd's secret scopes are shared, private or all; Runtime scopes by label, id or app.

picks.situation: A credential that must work for a non-HTTP service
picks.why: The proxy pattern is HTTP-shaped everywhere. If the credential is for a database or another raw protocol, it has to live in the machine, and boxd is the clearest about which secrets are host-bound and which are injected.

gotchas: InstaBox secrets only load in login shells: systemd units and `bash -c` do not see them.
An InstaBox snapshot includes saved Claude, Codex, git and SSH logins, so a snapshot can be a credential leak.
boxd wipes in-VM agent logins when a machine is shared, which breaks a running agent.
Runtime rewrites seven named headers only; an API that takes its key in the query string cannot use it.
A snapshot with a volume at Lizard embeds the volume's files, and anyone who can restore the snapshot can read them.
